assets.prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational
Asset type: landscape NDVI raster illustration for FAIRY 2.0's existing dark survey-image card.
Primary request: a very crisp, high-resolution simulated NDVI field image, like a UAV remote-sensing pseudocolor raster. This is a fictional DEMO illustration, not a sensor measurement.
Composition: one long rectangular agricultural field shown as a low oblique parallelogram, rising slightly toward the upper right, completely inside the frame. Keep generous dark charcoal (#202b30) margins. Field occupies about 85% of the image width and 55% of its height. No surrounding landscape, sky, plants, buildings, drones or perspective horizon. Thin pale field boundary. Subtle ridge-aligned microtexture within the field but no thick row stripes.
Field pattern for soybean disease context: predominantly vivid deep-to-mid green canopy, with fine irregular yellow and orange clusters concentrated in a broken belt toward the right half and a few small red stress pockets. Many sharply resolved pixel-like flecks and contiguous irregular clusters at multiple sizes, like a real orthomosaic NDVI product. Avoid blurry gradients, low-resolution smearing, smooth heatmap blobs, random speckle everywhere, or a simple grid of colored squares. Green about 80%, yellow/orange about 17%, red about 3%. Preserve natural, coherent patch shapes.
Palette: saturated NDVI red (low), yellow (middle), green (high); no cyan/purple. Background charcoal, no saturation elsewhere.
Style: precise remote-sensing visualization, flat color raster on the oblique ground plane, not a photograph and not a crop illustration. Sharp edges. Wide landscape image, roughly 3:2.
Text: no letters, no numbers, no legend, no logos, no watermarks. The app will add accurate English labels, a shared numeric legend and 'Simulated example' outside the image.
Constraints: produce exactly one complete field image. Do not create a collage or before/after panel. The synthetic patch positions are illustrative and must not imply GPS or diagnosis.
